claims.text: In Restate, each virtual object has a unique key (e.g., a session ID) and all handler calls on that object are serialized.

In Restate, each ctx.run() call is journaled before execution; if the handler crashes, Restate re-invokes it and replays the journal, skipping already-executed runs, giving exactly-once semantics without idempotency keys in application code.
Restate deduplicates requests using the Idempotency-Key header and stores completed responses for 24 hours by default, returning them when the same key is invoked again.
Without an explicit idempotency key, Restate's controlled idempotent sharding protects only retries of the same in-flight request, not separate requests sent later.
ZenML recommends modeling agent sessions as Restate Virtual Objects keyed by a session, customer, or task ID: requests for the same key run one at a time while different keys run in parallel.
Restate SDKs expose ctx.run-style durable steps, built-in key-value state, durable timers, idempotency keys, and callback waits called awakeables.
Temporal records an event history per workflow (activity scheduled, started, completed); on replay the workflow code re-executes deterministically and completed steps return their recorded results.

Temporal guidance for GPU-backed agents is to put GPU-bound or side-effecting operations in activities, not workflow code, because workflow code must be deterministic and fast since it replays on every worker restart.
Temporal's heartbeat_timeout (e.g., 60s, with heartbeats every 30s) lets Temporal detect a dead GPU worker (spot preemption, OOM, crash) within one timeout interval and reschedule the activity.
The Spheron article says Temporal gets exactly-once semantics via idempotency keys, Inngest via step IDs, and Restate natively.

Temporal workflow code must be deterministic (no Date.now(), random, or direct HTTP); every non-deterministic operation must move into an Activity, and the author estimates about two weeks to production versus an afternoon to attach a LangGraph checkpointer.

Because a model call can return a different answer each time, it must be treated as a recorded step rather than part of replayed workflow logic; changing workflow code while runs are open can make old histories replay down a mismatched path.
Inngest's step.run() persists each step result; if a workflow fails at the analysis step it resumes there, and the planning and search steps are not re-executed, so each LLM call is paid for once.
Inngest's step.waitForEvent() suspends a workflow for human approval (the example uses a 7-day timeout, matched on data.draftId) without consuming compute while waiting.

Inngest step.run accepts per-step retry options, e.g., retries: 5 with exponential backoff from 1s to a 5m maximum; if the API rate-limits on the 15th contact, the first 14 enrichments are not re-run.
Inngest's function-level concurrency option caps parallel GPU calls, and retries are per step, so only the failed step is retried.

Inngest describes durable agents as workflows whose next step is chosen by a model, with each model call and tool call running as a step, and durable endpoints as HTTP endpoints that survive intermittent errors.

In Inngest, an agent that picks tool calls at runtime needs each call in its own durable step; grouping several calls in one step makes them share a recovery boundary, and the Pro plan ($99/month) includes 1 million executions and 100 concurrent steps.
Hatchet's ordinary tasks are at-least-once, so idempotency remains the developer's responsibility unless durable boundaries are used carefully.
DBOS is durable execution as a library that checkpoints into an existing Postgres database.

A workflow replay that re-sends a provider call without the same idempotency key causes a second charge, email, or ticket; the idempotency key must be reused on the retry, and neither Temporal nor Inngest does this automatically.
A step that timed out may have actually succeeded before retry, so refunds, emails, and account changes need idempotency keys or check-before-write at the receiving system.
A human-in-the-loop gate suspends the agent at a named checkpoint, writes full state to the log, releases the process thread, and resumes when approval arrives, whether minutes or days later.

A Vercel AI SDK comparison states WorkflowAgent adds process-restart recovery, per-step tool retries, and durable suspension for long approval waits over the in-memory ToolLoopAgent, but recommends keeping ToolLoopAgent for short synchronous interactions.
Decagon's glossary describes customer-support uses such as refunds awaiting manager sign-off or warehouse confirmation, and says the event history doubles as an AI audit trail.
